pages.text: Ships and boats talk on the $(thing)VHF marine channels$(), 156-162 MHz. A marine radio has no dial: you pick a $(thing)channel$() and it knows the frequencies. Channel $(thing)16$() is distress, safety and calling: every ship listens there. Channel $(thing)9$() is for hailing other boats; then you move to a working channel such as 68 or 72.$(br2)Marine radios need no ham callsign.

pages.title: Marine Handheld
pages.text: 5 W or 1 W, with a 16/9 key and dual watch. Sneak and use it for the keys and channel; hold right click to talk. It runs on a small battery and charges in a desk charger like the other handhelds.

pages.title: Marine Radio
pages.text: The fixed-mount radio for a boat's console or a harbour office: 25 W or 1 W, with a hand mic on a cord (sneak and use). It needs power and a VHF antenna, and it works on a ship that sails.

pages.title: The keys
pages.text: $(thing)16/9$(): to channel 16, press again for 9, and once more back to the channel you were on.$(br)$(thing)H/L$(): high or low power. Use 1 W for ships close by; channels 13, 15, 17 and 67 are always 1 W.$(br)$(thing)DW$() (dual watch): listen to your channel and 16 at once. While 16 is busy you hear only 16.

pages.title: Special channels
pages.text: Some channels are $(thing)duplex$(): you transmit on the ship frequency and hear the coast station 4.6 MHz higher, so two ships on one cannot hear each other. The $(thing)WX$() channels are NOAA weather and only receive. Channel 70 is DSC, digital calling only: no voice.$(br2)Servers use the US channel plan unless set to the international one.
Built like the commercial radios, on waterproof wire.
